It works on any JavaScript runtime: Cloudflare Workers, Fastly Compute, Deno, Bun, Vercel, AWS Lambda, Lambda@Edge, and Node.js. Fast, but not only fast. ```ts import { Hono } from 'hono' const app = new Hono() app.get('/', (c) => c.text('Hono!')) export default app ``` ## Quick Start ```bash npm create hono@latest ``` ## Features - **Ultrafast** 🚀 - The router `RegExpRouter` is really fast. Not using linear loops. Fast. - **Lightweight** 🪶 - The `hono/tiny` preset is under 12kB. Hono has zero dependencies and uses only the Web Standard API. - **Multi-runtime** 🌍 - Works on Cloudflare Workers, Fastly Compute, Deno, Bun, AWS Lambda, Lambda@Edge, or Node.js. The same code runs on all platforms. - **Batteries Included** 🔋 - Hono has built-in middleware, custom middleware, and third-party middleware. Batteries included. - **Delightful DX** 😃 - Super clean APIs. First-class TypeScript support. Now, we've got "Types". ## Documentation The documentation is available on [hono.dev](https://hono.dev). ## Migration The migration guide is available on [docs/MIGRATION.md](docs/MIGRATION.md). ## Communication [X](https://x.com/honojs) and [Discord channel](https://discord.gg/KMh2eNSdxV) are available. ## Contributing Contributions Welcome! # Contributor Covenant Code of Conduct

## Our Pledge

We as members, contributors, and leaders pledge to make participation in our
community a harassment-free experience for everyone, regardless of age, body
size, visible or invisible disability, ethnicity, sex characteristics, gender
identity and expression, level of experience, education, socio-economic status,
nationality, personal appearance, race, religion, or sexual identity
and orientation.

We pledge to act and interact in ways that contribute to an open, welcoming,
diverse, inclusive, and healthy community.

## Our Standards

Examples of behavior that contributes to a positive environment for our
community include:

- Demonstrating empathy and kindness toward other people
- Being respectful of differing opinions, viewpoints, and experiences
- Giving and gracefully accepting constructive feedback
- Accepting responsibility and apologizing to those affected by our mistakes,
  and learning from the experience
- Focusing on what is best not just for us as individuals, but for the
  overall community

Examples of unacceptable behavior include:

- The use of sexualized language or imagery, and sexual attention or
  advances of any kind
- Trolling, insulting or derogatory comments, and personal or political attacks
- Public or private harassment
- Publishing others' private information, such as a physical or email
  address, without their explicit permission
- Other conduct which could reasonably be considered inappropriate in a
  professional setting

## Enforcement Responsibilities

Community leaders are responsible for clarifying and enforcing our standards of
acceptable behavior and will take appropriate and fair corrective action in
response to any behavior that they deem inappropriate, threatening, or offensive,
or harmful.

Community leaders have the right and responsibility to remove, edit, or reject
comments, commits, code, wiki edits, issues, and other contributions that are
not aligned to this Code of Conduct, and will communicate reasons for moderation
decisions when appropriate.

## Scope

This Code of Conduct applies within all community spaces, and also applies when
an individual is officially representing the community in public spaces.
Examples of representing our community include using an official e-mail address,
posting via an official social media account, or acting as an appointed
representative at an online or offline event.

## Enforcement

Instances of abusive, harassing, or otherwise unacceptable behavior may be
reported to the community leaders responsible for enforcement at
yusuke@kamawada.com.
All complaints will be reviewed and investigated promptly and fairly.

All community leaders are obligated to respect the privacy and security of the
reporter of any incident.

## Enforcement Guidelines

Community leaders will follow these Community Impact Guidelines in determining
the consequences for any action they deem in violation of this Code of Conduct:

### 1. Correction

**Community Impact**: Use of inappropriate language or other behavior deemed
unprofessional or unwelcome in the community.

**Consequence**: A private, written warning from community leaders, providing
clarity around the nature of the violation and an explanation of why the
behavior was inappropriate. A public apology may be requested.

### 2. Warning

**Community Impact**: A violation through a single incident or a series
of actions.

**Consequence**: A warning with consequences for continued behavior. No
interaction with the people involved, including unsolicited interaction with
those enforcing the Code of Conduct, for a specified period of time. This
includes avoiding interactions in community spaces as well as external channels
like social media. Violating these terms may lead to a temporary or
permanent ban.

### 3. Temporary Ban

**Community Impact**: A serious violation of community standards, including
sustained inappropriate behavior.

**Consequence**: A temporary ban from any sort of interaction or public
communication with the community for a specified period of time. No public or
private interaction with the people involved, including unsolicited interaction
with those enforcing the Code of Conduct, is allowed during this period.
Violating these terms may lead to a permanent ban.

### 4. Permanent Ban

**Community Impact**: Demonstrating a pattern of violation of the community
standards, including sustained inappropriate behavior, harassment of an
individual, or aggression toward or disparagement of classes of individuals.

**Consequence**: A permanent ban from any sort of public interaction within
the community.

## Attribution

version 2.0, available at
https://www.contributor-covenant.org/version/2/0/code_of_conduct.html.

Community Impact Guidelines were inspired by [Mozilla's code of conduct
enforcement ladder](https://github.com/mozilla/diversity).

# Contribution Guide

Contributions Welcome! We will be glad for your help.
You can contribute in the following ways.

- Create an Issue - Propose a new feature. Report a bug.
- Pull Request - Fix a bug or typo. Refactor the code.
- Create third-party middleware - See instructions below.
- Share - Share your thoughts on the Blog, X, and others.
- Make your application - Please try to use Hono.

Note:
This project is started by Yusuke Wada ([@yusukebe](https://github.com/yusukebe)) for the hobby proposal.
It was just for fun. For now, this stance has not been changed basically.
I want to write the code as I like.
So, if you propose great ideas, but I do not appropriate them, the idea may not be accepted.

Although, don't worry!
Hono is tested well, polished by the contributors, and used by many developers. And I'll try my best to make Hono cool and hot, beautiful, and ultrafast.

## AI Usage Policy

You may use AI to contribute, but it must never waste a maintainer's time or make their work unpleasant.

To enforce this, and regardless of whether AI was actually used, a maintainer may close your PR without notice and block your account.

## Installing dependencies

The `honojs/hono` project uses [pnpm](https://pnpm.io/) as its package manager, and [Bun](https://bun.sh/) to run the build and some of the tests. Developers should install both.

After that, please install the dependency environment.

```bash
pnpm install --frozen-lockfile
```

## PRs

Please ensure your PR passes tests with `pnpm run test`.

## Third-party middleware

Third-party middleware is not in the core.
It is allowed to depend on other libraries or work only in specific environments, such as Cloudflare Workers. For example:

- GraphQL Server middleware
- Firebase Auth middleware
- Sentry middleware

You can make a third-party middleware by yourself.
It may be under the "honojs organization" and distributed in the `@honojs` namespace.

The monorepo "[honojs/middleware](https://github.com/honojs/middleware)" manages these middleware.
If you want to do it, create an issue about your middleware.

## Local Development

```bash
git clone git@github.com:honojs/hono.git && cd hono && pnpm install --frozen-lockfile
```

# Maintaining

Notes for maintainers of this repository.

## Adapters

Runtime adapters live in `adapters/*` and are published as separate packages (`@hono/bun`, ...). Each directory is a pnpm workspace package. The root package is `hono` itself.

### Layout

```
adapters/bun/
  src/            # imports hono via `hono`, `hono/ws`, ... (workspace link)
  src/*.test.ts   # runs with `bun test`
  package.json    # peerDependencies: hono >=x.y.z
  vite.config.ts  # `vp pack` config (ESM only)
```

### Commands

From the repository root:

```sh
pnpm run build:adapters   # build every adapter
pnpm run test:adapters    # tsc + bun test for every adapter
pnpm --filter @hono/bun run test
```

CI runs `ci-adapters.yml` for changes under `adapters/**` (and `src/**`, since adapters depend on `hono`). The main `ci.yml` skips changes that only touch `adapters/**`.

### Versioning

- Adapter versions are independent from `hono`. Do not bump them when `hono` is released.
- Compatibility is expressed by `peerDependencies.hono` in each adapter. Raise the lower bound when an adapter starts using something newer.
- Git tags are `@hono/<name>@<version>`. Only `hono` uses `v<version>`.

### Releasing

```sh
pnpm run release:adapter bun patch   # or minor, major, or an exact x.y.z
```

This bumps `adapters/bun/package.json`, commits, creates an annotated tag `@hono/bun@<version>` and pushes. The `release.yml` workflow then packs the adapter and runs `npm stage publish`. Approve the staged version on npm (2FA) to make it public.

At the end the script prints a release-note draft built from the commits that touched `adapters/bun` since the previous adapter tag, plus a prefilled GitHub "new release" link. Creating a GitHub Release is optional.

### JSR

`@hono/deno` and `@hono/netlify` are also published to JSR. Each has a `deno.json` that is the JSR package config: its `imports`
map `hono` to `jsr:@hono/hono`, and its `version` stays `0.0.0` like the root `jsr.json`.
The `release.yml` workflow writes the version from the tag into `deno.json` and runs `deno publish` when the tagged adapter has a `deno.json`.
Before the first release, create the package on jsr.io under the `@hono` scope and link the `honojs/hono`
repository so the workflow can publish with OIDC. `deno publish --dry-run --set-version 0.0.1` in the adapter directory checks the package locally (`--set-version` is fine for a dry run; the real publish needs the version in `deno.json`).

Tests under `adapters/deno/test` run on Deno (`pnpm --filter @hono/deno run test:deno`) with `test/deno.json`,
which maps `hono` to the working tree instead.

### Adding a new adapter

1. Copy `adapters/bun` as `adapters/<name>` and adjust `package.json` (`name`, `description`) and the sources.
2. The workspace picks it up automatically (`pnpm-workspace.yaml` has `adapters/*`).
3. Add it to the corresponding `src/adapter/<name>` with `@deprecated` on each export, pointing to the new package.
4. **First publish is manual.** See below.
5. From the second release on, use `pnpm run release:adapter <name> <bump>`.

#### First publish of a new adapter

npm only allows a Trusted Publisher on a package that already exists, so the first version is published from a maintainer's machine:

1. Set the version in `adapters/<name>/package.json` and merge it.
2. Build it: `pnpm --filter @hono/<name> run build` (`pnpm publish` does not build).
3. In `adapters/<name>`, run `pnpm publish --access public` with your npm 2FA.
4. On npmjs.com, open the package settings and add a Trusted Publisher: repository `honojs/hono`, workflow `release.yml`.

# Migration Guide

## v4.3.11 to v4.4.0

### `deno.land/x` to JSR

There is no breaking change, but we no longer publish the module from `deno.land/x`. If you want to use Hono on Deno, use JSR instead of it.

If you migrate, replace the path `deno.land/x` with JSR's.

```ts
// From
import { Hono } from 'https://deno.land/x/hono/mod.ts'

// To
import { Hono } from 'jsr:@hono/hono'
```

You can see more details on our website: https://hono.dev/getting-started/deno

## v3.12.x to v4.0.0

There are some breaking changes.

### Removal of deprecated features

- AWS Lambda Adapter - `LambdaFunctionUrlRequestContext` is obsolete. Use `ApiGatewayRequestContextV2` instead.
- Next.js Adapter - `hono/nextjs` is obsolete. Use `hono/vercel` instead.
- Context - `c.jsonT()` is obsolete. Use `c.json()` instead.
- Context - `c.stream()` and `c.streamText()` are obsolete. Use `stream()` and `streamText()` in `hono/streaming` instead.
- Context - `c.env()` is obsolete. Use `getRuntimeKey()` in `hono/adapter` instead.
- Hono - `app.showRoutes()` is obsolete. Use `showRoutes()` in `hono/dev` instead.
- Hono - `app.routerName` is obsolete. Use `getRouterName()` in `hono/dev` instead.
- Hono - `app.head()` is no longer used. `app.get()` implicitly handles the HEAD method.
- Hono - `app.handleEvent()` is obsolete. Use `app.fetch()` instead.
- HonoRequest - `req.cookie()` is obsolete. Use `getCookie()` in `hono/cookie` instead.
- HonoRequest - `headers()`, `body()`, `bodyUsed()`, `integrity()`, `keepalive()`, `referrer()`, and `signal()` are obsolete. Use the equivalent properties on `req.raw` such as `req.raw.headers`.

### `serveStatic` in Cloudflare Workers Adapter requires `manifest`

If you use the Cloudflare Workers adapter's `serve-static`, you should specify the `manifest` option.

```ts
import manifest from '__STATIC_CONTENT_MANIFEST'

// ...

app.use('/static/*', serveStatic({ root: './assets', manifest }))
```

### Others

- The default value of the `docType` option in JSX Renderer Middleware is now `true`.
- `FC` in `hono/jsx` does not pass `children`. Use `PropsWithChildren`.
- Some Mime Types are removed https://github.com/honojs/hono/pull/2119.
- Types for chaining routes with middleware matter: https://github.com/honojs/hono/pull/2046.
- Types for the validator matter: https://github.com/honojs/hono/pull/2130.

## v2.7.8 to v3.0.0

There are some breaking changes.
In addition to the following, type mismatches may occur.

### `c.req` is now `HonoRequest`

`c.req` becomes `HonoRequest`, not `Request`.
Although APIs are almost the same, if you want to access `Request`, use `c.req.raw`.

```ts
app.post('/', async (c) => {
  const metadata = c.req.raw.cf?.hostMetadata?
  ...
})
```

### StaticRouter is obsolete

You can't use `StaticRouter`.

### Validator has been changed

Previous Validator Middleware is obsolete.
You can still use `hono/validator`, but the API has been changed.
See [the document](https://hono.dev).

### `serveStatic` is provided from the Adapter

Serve Static Middleware is obsolete. Use Adapters instead.

```ts
// For Cloudflare Workers
import { serveStatic } from 'hono/cloudflare-workers'

// For Bun
// import { serveStatic } from 'hono/bun'

// For Deno
// import { serveStatic } from 'npm:hono/deno'

// ...

app.get('/static/*', serveStatic({ root: './' }))
```

### `serveStatic` for Cloudflare Workers "Service Worker mode" is obsolete

For Cloudflare Workers, the `serveStatic` is obsolete in Service Worker mode.

Note: Service Worker mode is that using `app.fire()`.
We recommend use "Module Worker" mode with `export default app`.

### Use `type` to define the Generics for `new Hono`

You must use `type` to define the Generics for `new Hono`. Do not use `interface`.

```ts
// Should use `type`
type Bindings = {
  TOKEN: string
}

const app = new Hono<{ Bindings: Bindings }>()
```

## v2.7.1 - v2.x.x

### Current Validator Middleware is deprecated

At the next major version, Validator Middleware will be changed with "breaking changes". Therefore, the current Validator Middleware will be deprecated; please use 3rd-party Validator libraries such as [Zod](https://zod.dev) or [TypeBox](https://github.com/sinclairzx81/typebox).

```ts
import * as z from 'zod'

//...

const schema = z.object({
  title: z.string().max(100),
})

app.post('/posts', async (c) => {
  const body = await c.req.parseBody()
  const res = schema.safeParse(body)
  if (!res.success) {
    return c.text('Invalid!', 400)
  }
  return c.text('Valid!')
})
```

## v2.2.5 to v2.3.0

There is a breaking change associated with the security update.

### Basic Auth Middleware and Bearer Auth Middleware

If you are using Basic Auth and Bearer Auth in your Handler (nested), change as follows:

```ts
app.use('/auth/*', async (c, next) => {
  const auth = basicAuth({ username: c.env.USERNAME, password: c.env.PASSWORD })
  return auth(c, next) // Older: `await auth(c, next)`
})
```

## v2.0.9 to v2.1.0

There are two BREAKING CHANGES.

### `c.req.parseBody` does not parse JSON, text, and ArrayBuffer

**DO NOT** use `c.req.parseBody` for parsing **JSON**, **text**, or **ArrayBuffer**.

`c.req.parseBody` now only parses FormData with content type `multipart/form` or `application/x-www-form-urlencoded`. If you want to parse JSON, text, or ArrayBuffer, use `c.req.json()`, `c.req.text()`, or `c.req.arrayBuffer()`.

```ts
// `multipart/form` or `application/x-www-form-urlencoded`
const data = await c.req.parseBody()

const jsonData = await c.req.json() // for JSON body
const text = await c.req.text() // for text body
const arrayBuffer = await c.req.arrayBuffer() // for ArrayBuffer
```

### The arguments of Generics for `new Hono` have been changed

Now, the constructor of "Hono" receives `Variables` and `Bindings`.
"Bindings" is for types of environment variables for Cloudflare Workers. "Variables" is for types of `c.set`/`c.get`

```ts
type Bindings = {
  KV: KVNamespace
  Storage: R2Bucket
}

type WebClient = {
  user: string
  pass: string
}

type Variables = {
  client: WebClient
}

const app = new Hono<{ Variables: Variables; Bindings: Bindings }>()

app.get('/foo', (c) => {
  const client = c.get('client') // client is WebClient
  const kv = c.env.KV // kv is KVNamespace
  //...
})
```

## v1.6.4 to v2.0.0

There are many BREAKING CHANGES. Please follow the instructions below.

### The way to import Middleware on Deno has been changed

**DO NOT** import middleware from `hono/mod.ts`.

```ts
import { Hono, poweredBy } from 'https://deno.land/x/hono/mod.ts' // <--- NG
```

`hono/mod.ts` does not export middleware.
To import middleware, use `hono/middleware.ts`:

```ts
import { Hono } from 'https://deno.land/x/hono/mod.ts'
import { poweredBy, basicAuth } from 'https://deno.land/x/hono/middleware.ts'
```

### Cookie middleware is obsolete

**DO NOT** use `cookie` middleware.

```ts
import { cookie } from 'hono/cookie' // <--- Obsolete!
```

You do not have to use Cookie middleware to parse or set cookies.
They become default functions:

```ts
// Parse cookie
app.get('/entry/:id', (c) => {
  const value = c.req.cookie('name')
  ...
})
```

```ts
app.get('/', (c) => {
  c.cookie('delicious_cookie', 'choco')
  return c.text('Do you like cookie?')
})
```

### Body parse middleware is obsolete

**DO NOT** use `body-parse` middleware.

```ts
import { bodyParse } from 'hono/body-parse' // <--- Obsolete!
```

You do not have to use Body parse middleware to parse the request body. Use `c.req.parseBody()` method instead.

```ts
// Parse Request body
app.post('', (c) => {
  const body = c.req.parseBody()
  ...
})
```

### GraphQL Server middleware is obsolete

**DO NOT** use `graphql-server` middleware.

```ts
import { graphqlServer } from 'hono/graphql-server' // <--- Obsolete!
```

It might be distributed as third-party middleware.

### Mustache middleware is obsolete

**DO NOT** use `mustache` middleware.

```ts
import { mustache } from 'hono/mustache' // <--- Obsolete!
```

It will no longer be implemented.

report.overview: Hono is a TypeScript web framework whose application boundary is a standard Request-to-Response fetch handler. It serves developers building APIs and web applications across JavaScript runtimes, with interchangeable routers, composable middleware, typed clients, JSX rendering, streaming, and static generation. At commit f23b146afcec63606144cde50b5fbd360dd60238, the repository also maintains independently packaged runtime adapters alongside deprecated in-package adapters.
report.agent_prompt:
Onboard to Hono at commit f23b146afcec63606144cde50b5fbd360dd60238. Treat this brief as a bounded source investigation, not exhaustive coverage or evidence that tests pass. Tests and CI were inspected, not executed. Verify the checkout and relevant code before acting. Under the original investigation authority, use only read/search operations on public tracked source, prefix shell commands with rtk, and do not execute repository code, install dependencies, build, test, access the network, or write files. Never inspect secrets, environment files, credentials, or keys. A subsequent implementation task needs its own applicable authorization.

Start with package.json, jsr.json, src/index.ts, src/hono.ts, src/hono-base.ts, src/router.ts, src/compose.ts, src/context.ts, and src/request.ts. Hono is a library, not a deployed application with a fixed route catalog. Applications register handlers through get/post/on/use and supply runtime bindings and execution context to fetch. HonoBase registers route metadata and dispatches requests; the default Hono chooses SmartRouter with RegExpRouter and TrieRouter. SmartRouter selects its active router on the first match and then rejects additional route registration. basePath clones share the router and routes array.

Trace changes through both dispatch branches: a single matched handler bypasses compose, while multiple handlers use onion-style next dispatch. compose updates req.routeIndex, rejects repeated next calls, and installs returned responses on Context. HEAD dispatches through GET and returns a bodyless response. Context lazily constructs HonoRequest, owns request-local variables, merges response headers, and exposes bindings. Preserve response finalization and Set-Cookie handling.

For input changes, read src/validator/validator.ts and src/request.ts together. Validators parse supported targets, can return an early Response, or save transformed values for req.valid. Body readers cache representations; consuming req.raw directly can prevent cloneRawRequest from reconstructing a consumed body. The hc client in src/client/client.ts builds paths through proxies, serializes forms, JSON, query parameters and cookies, and supports injected fetch and WebSocket implementations.

For persistence, inspect cache middleware and SSG separately. cache uses the runtime Cache API, varies keys by configured headers, hashes QUERY bodies and metadata, and bypasses Authorization requests and unsuitable responses. Its default asynchronous writes require executionCtx.waitUntil. SSG invokes application handlers, expands dynamic parameters, applies ordered plugins, checks lexical output containment, and writes through an injected filesystem interface. Handler execution during generation can have application side effects.

Read docs/MAINTAINING.md before adapter work. adapters contains separately versioned workspace packages importing hono; src/adapter retains compatibility implementations. Read the corresponding package manifest, adapter implementation, Vite configuration and tests. New exports must remain consistent between npm and JSR; Vite validates these maps and emits ESM, CJS and declarations.

For a later authorized change, prefer small diffs and the existing pnpm scripts. Inspect focused colocated tests first, then the root type-checking test script and relevant runtime or adapter script. Declaration tests require built artifacts and create temporary consumer projects. Do not equate mocked cache or Lambda tests with production-provider verification. Report actual checks and limitations, and label security hypotheses explicitly.

system_map.summary: The public entrypoint exports Hono and supporting types, while HonoBase owns registration and dispatch. Request and Context wrap standard web objects, and runtime adapters translate platform boundaries. Storage behavior inspected here belongs to optional cache and SSG facilities. Distribution includes npm ESM/CJS/declarations, JSR source exports, and separate adapter packages.

claims.claim: src/index.ts exports Hono, Context, HonoRequest types, handler/environment types, and typed client inference utilities.
The default Hono extends HonoBase and uses SmartRouter with RegExpRouter followed by TrieRouter unless options.router is supplied.
HonoBase supplies dynamically initialized HTTP method registration, on(), use(), route metadata, and the fetch application boundary.
Context owns bindings, request-local variable storage, response state and execution context; it lazily constructs HonoRequest.
The root package distributes dist with ESM, CommonJS and declaration entrypoints; Vite emits these as three unbundled outputs.
The pnpm workspace contains the root and adapters packages; @hono/aws-lambda and @hono/bun expose ESM dist entrypoints and require hono >=4.13.9 as a peer.
Optional persistence uses the runtime Cache API for responses and an injected FileSystemModule for generated files.
Root scripts define type-check-plus-Vitest testing, runtime-specific tests, adapter tests, and Vite-plus packaging with publint.
Release automation distinguishes v* root tags from @hono/* adapter tags, stages npm publication with provenance, and separately publishes JSR packages.

feature_catalog.summary: The user-facing product is a framework API and exported modules rather than a fixed application route set. Routing, responses, middleware and validation form the server surface. Typed clients, JSX, streaming, WebSockets and static generation extend it into full web application development. The export-map inventory is broader than the implementation paths examined in detail.

claims.claim: Applications register get/post/put/delete/options/patch/query/all handlers, arbitrary method/path combinations through on(), and path-scoped middleware through use().
route() groups Hono applications, basePath() prefixes registration, and mount() integrates another Request handler with configurable request replacement and arguments.
Context exposes text, JSON, HTML, redirect and custom-body response construction; onError() and notFound() customize application failures.
validator() supports JSON, form, query, path parameter, header and cookie targets, allowing transformed data or an early Response.
hc() supplies proxy-generated HTTP calls, $url/$path helpers and $ws connections, with form, JSON, query, parameter, header and cookie inputs.
The JSR export map exposes authentication, IP restriction, body limits, cache, compression, CORS, CSRF, ETag and trailing-slash middleware.
Additional exported middleware covers timeouts, timing, logging, method handling, request IDs, language selection, secure headers, JSON formatting and middleware combinations.
Hono JSX exports components, context, hooks, Suspense and ErrorBoundary; the DOM package additionally exports render, portals, flushSync and form-state hooks.
stream() returns a streaming Response; streamSSE() adds SSE headers and writeSSE() formats data, event, id and retry fields.
toSSG() generates route output files with configurable concurrency, MIME extensions and plugins; redirectPlugin() converts redirects into HTML pages.
Bun and Deno adapters export static serving, SSG, WebSocket and connection helpers; Cloudflare Workers exports static serving, WebSocket upgrade and connection information.
Lambda offers buffered handle() and streamHandle(); Vercel forwards Requests directly, Netlify passes its context in bindings, and Service Worker handling can fall back to network fetch on 404.
tiny uses PatternRouter, while quick uses SmartRouter with LinearRouter and TrieRouter.

data_flow.summary: Incoming Requests pass through path extraction and router matching into a per-request Context. Middleware and validators progressively attach state before response construction. Clients and adapters serialize or translate data at the outer boundaries. Cache writes and SSG files are separate optional output paths with different ownership and lifetime.

claims.claim: fetch(request, env, executionCtx) forwards the method and supplied runtime values into #dispatch(), which extracts the path, matches routes and constructs Context.
Router results carry handler tuples and either parameter indexes with a stash or direct parameter maps; HonoRequest resolves the active route's parameters and decodes their values.
compose dispatch assigns req.routeIndex before each handler, calls the next handler recursively and places returned responses into Context.
HonoRequest caches consumed body representations and rebuilds alternate representations through Response while retaining the original media type except for FormData.
Validation parses the selected boundary, awaits validationFunc(), returns Response results immediately, and stores other results through addValidatedData() for valid().
Context JSON responses stringify objects and supply application/json; #newResponse combines existing/prepared headers, explicit headers and status.
ClientRequestImpl serializes forms or JSON, substitutes path parameters, appends query parameters and invokes supplied fetch or global fetch; GET and HEAD omit request bodies.
Lambda EventProcessor builds an HTTPS Request from event path/domain/query/headers, decodes base64 bodies, then serializes the Response to text or base64 with platform cookie handling.
Cache keys encode the logical key, method and configured header variants; QUERY additionally hashes representation metadata and body bytes within a configured size ceiling.
SSG routes become application Responses, then text or ArrayBuffer content, MIME-derived file paths and filesystem writes after output-containment validation.

behavior_traces.summary: Source reads followed registration and first-request routing, validated requests, cache persistence, Lambda translation and static generation. These traces describe function order and branches rather than executed observations. The default router becomes fixed after its first match. SSG executes application handlers as part of both route discovery and output production.

claims.claim: Startup registration: new Hono() calls HonoBase's constructor, initializes registration functions, selects SmartRouter, and app.get()/use() call #addRoute() to append metadata and router entries.

First request: fetch() → #dispatch() → getPath() → SmartRouter.match(); SmartRouter replays stored routes into candidates, skips UnsupportedPathError, and replaces match with the selected router's bound implementation.

Single-handler GET: #dispatch() invokes the handler directly; a returned Response is delivered and Promise rejection reaches #handleError(). For a Promise resolving without a response, a finalized Context returns c.res; otherwise notFound is used. A synchronous nullish return falls back to notFound.

Validated POST: compose.dispatch() invokes validator('json') → req.json() → cached text → JSON.parse() → validationFunc(); transformed output enters addValidatedData(), next() reaches the handler, and c.json() serializes its response.
Malformed JSON: validator catches body parsing failure and throws HTTPException(400); compose catches Error instances and passes them to onError, while the default handler uses getResponse().

Cache hit: cache middleware checks method and Authorization, computes a QUERY digest when needed, generates the key, opens caches, matches it and returns a new Response without calling downstream handlers.
Cache miss and persistence: cache.match() misses → await next() → status/Vary/Cache-Control/Set-Cookie checks → response.clone() → awaited cache.put() or executionCtx.waitUntil(cache.put()).

Lambda request: handle(app) chooses getProcessor(), calls createRequest(), passes event/requestContext/lambdaContext to app.fetch(), then calls createResult(); request-construction TypeErrors become 400 results.

Static generation: toSSG() combines hooks → fetchRoutesContent() filters routes and calls app.fetch() for metadata → parameter expansion calls app.request() → response hooks transform/filter content → saveContentToFile() creates directories and writes files.

SSE output: streamSSE() constructs TransformStream/SSEStreamingApi, sets protocol headers and starts run(); callback writeSSE() escapes line structure and writes framed events, and run() closes the stream in finally.

testing_signals.summary: Tests and CI were inspected, not executed; no passing result or measured coverage is asserted. The bounded inspection found Vitest unit/type tests, JSDOM rendering tests, runtime projects and adapter suites. CI schedules build, checks and several runtime jobs, but configured jobs are not execution evidence. Mocked platform tests and coverage exclusions limit what these sources establish.

claims.claim: The root test script first runs tsc against tsconfig.spec.json, then vp test --run; the spec configuration enables Vitest globals and Hono JSX.
Vitest includes colocated src tests and build tests in main, imports runtime project configurations, and excludes standalone *.case.test.* files from main discovery.
Coverage uses V8 with JSON/text/HTML reports and excludes runtime-tests, benchmarks, perf-measures and specified compile-time type files.
Hono tests explicitly separate requests without middleware from composed requests and inspect status, body, response headers, bindings and 404 behavior.
compose tests exercise request-local state, post-next response-header mutation, returned JSON and handlers returning Promises from non-async functions.
Type tests use expectTypeOf and Equal/Expect assertions for bindings, variables, validated inputs and inferred route schema; validator tests assert query acceptance and rejection.
DOM tests import JSDOM and test element creation, children, keys and refs; two Vitest projects run DOM-related suites with different JSX import sources.
Cache unit tests replace global caches with a Map-backed MockCache, so the inspected assertions establish intended key/hit behavior rather than real provider persistence.
SSG path tests assert lexical containment across traversal, partial-prefix names, current directories, parent directories, Windows drives and UNC roots.
Lambda backpressure tests stub awslambda, stream into a delayed Node Writable, assert bounded read-ahead and completion, and exercise mid-stream failure reporting.
Published declaration tests create a temporary consumer project, symlink Hono, invoke tsc through spawnSync and clean up; they test packaging behavior beyond source-only type assertions.

Main CI configures check/build/test, Deno JSX/runtime testing, Bun including Windows, Fastly, workerd and a Node version matrix; a later setup-node step also appears in the matrix job and merits checking before assuming its actual runtime version.

Adapter CI runs root and adapter builds, adapter tests and Deno adapter tests for selected path changes; PR jobs also configure type/bundle measurements and HTTP benchmarks without providing results in these files.

risk_map.summary: These are source observations and explicitly labeled hypotheses, not confirmed vulnerabilities. Authentication, outbound fetch, file access, body consumption and response caching are sensitive boundaries. Shared routing state and duplicated adapter generations increase compatibility concerns. Partial test inspection cannot establish that any critical flow is wholly untested.

claims.claim: Routing registration becomes immutable after SmartRouter's first match, and basePath clones share its router and route list; adding routes after serving begins can throw across related instances.
Single-handler dispatch bypasses compose, whereas multi-handler dispatch enforces Context finalization; changes to return/error semantics must account for both paths.
bodyLimit trusts Content-Length when Transfer-Encoding is absent; otherwise it consumes and buffers chunks before invoking downstream handlers.

Hypothesis: callers constructing Requests with inconsistent Content-Length could defeat an actual-byte limit on the trusted-length branch; whether a deployment permits this depends on its ingress runtime.

CSRF protection applies to unsafe methods with form-compatible media types and allows the request if either Origin or Sec-Fetch-Site validation succeeds; it is not a universal check on every request type.

JWT middleware requires a configured algorithm and secret, accepts bearer headers or configured cookies, and places verified claims in jwtPayload; JWKS verification rejects symmetric algorithms and checks the allowlist and matching key algorithm.

JWKS verification performs fetch(options.jwks_uri, init), and JWK middleware can derive that URI from Context; outbound destination trust and fetch policy therefore belong to application configuration.
Cache bypasses Authorization requests and responses with Set-Cookie, private/no-cache/no-store or unsupported Vary; its default background write accesses executionCtx, which throws if absent.

Static serving rejects routed percent signs by default and suspicious decoded path segments, but configured path and rewriteRequestPath feed runtime file access; these callbacks/options are sensitive trust boundaries.

SSG enforces lexical output containment before filesystem writes; the inspected filesystem interface has no realpath or symlink-resolution operation, so physical containment is not established by this check.

SSG invokes application handlers for metadata and generated content, while createdDirs is module-global; generation lifecycle and handler side effects need attention when reusing an application or changing output directories.

proxy() forwards through supplied fetch or global fetch and can carry raw request credentials; strictConnectionProcessing optionally removes headers named by an inbound Connection header and validates their syntax.
The html template helper escapes ordinary string interpolation but accepts already-escaped values and exports raw; direct Context.html(string) also treats its input as HTML.
Build declaration tests shell out to tsc and write temporary files outside the repository; build/release workflows also perform publication, so executing tooling exceeds this read-only investigation.
The Bun adapter exists both as a separate package and as deprecated in-package exports scheduled for removal in v5, creating a compatibility maintenance boundary.

extension_points.summary: Hono extends chiefly through handlers, middleware, injectable routers and explicit exported modules. Runtime bindings and adapters keep platform concerns outside core dispatch. Factory and validator APIs preserve types while allowing application-specific behavior. SSG has an explicit ordered plugin interface, and build plugins enforce distribution conventions.

claims.claim: Custom routers implement Router<T> with name, add() and match(), then enter the default Hono through options.router.
Custom getPath(request, {env}) can alter routing boundaries; strict mode controls selection of normal versus non-strict path extraction.
Handler and MiddlewareHandler define Context/Next extension contracts; use() registers middleware with the ALL method.
Factory.createApp() merges default app options and invokes initApp; createMiddleware() preserves middleware typing and createHandlers() collects defined handlers.
validator() accepts an application validation function rather than prescribing a schema library, with runtime transformation and early-response behavior.
mount() supports custom optionHandler and replaceRequest functions to bridge other frameworks and runtime argument conventions.
The static-serving base accepts getContent, join and isDir implementations plus path rewriting, MIME overrides and found/not-found hooks.
SSGPlugin exposes beforeRequestHook, afterResponseHook and afterGenerateHook, with single or multiple functions; FileSystemModule abstracts mkdir and writeFile.
SSG plugin order is observable: redirectPlugin must precede defaultPlugin because the latter filters non-200 responses.
hc() accepts a custom query builder, per-request/base options and injected WebSocket factory; proxy() separately supports customFetch.
New adapters are workspace-discovered, separately versioned packages; maintainer instructions require corresponding deprecated src/adapter exports.
Packaging plugins validate npm/JSR export-map parity and transform emitted declarations, including removal of private fields and appendExportEmptyToDts.

agent_handoff.summary: Tests and CI were inspected, not executed, and this brief is a bounded inventory rather than exhaustive coverage. Begin edits from the relevant runtime path and its colocated tests, preserving public typing and packaging contracts. Adapter changes require attention to both separate packages and deprecated compatibility surfaces. The original task authorizes read/search only; the commands described here are references for a later authorized implementation task.

claims.claim: Read HonoBase, compose, Context and HonoRequest together for dispatch changes because they jointly own handler order, route indexes, response finalization and parsed input.
Preserve both single-handler and composed dispatch semantics and HEAD-to-GET behavior; the Hono test suite distinguishes composed and uncomposed requests.
Use the declared pnpm@12.6.0 package manager and existing scripts as the command reference; root test includes type checking, while runtime and adapter scripts have distinct scopes.

For a later authorized verification, inspect the smallest colocated suite first, then use root test and the affected runtime/adapter script; declaration tests additionally exercise a temporary external consumer and rely on dist/types behavior.
Keep new public exports synchronized between package.json and jsr.json because the build plugin checks parity in both directions.
Adapter work should begin with docs/MAINTAINING.md and the relevant package manifest/config; adapter versions and peer compatibility are independent of root Hono releases.
Do not consume req.raw bodies casually when later middleware or forwarding needs reconstruction: cloneRawRequest throws when the body was consumed without a HonoRequest cache.
Read SSG plugin order, route discovery and output containment before changing generation; custom plugins replace the default plugin list, and discovery invokes handlers.
Follow the established formatter settings: two spaces, no semicolons, single quotes, LF and print width 100; lint requires top-level type import conventions.

Treat observed assertions and CI steps as verification plans, not passing evidence: cache tests use mocked caches, Lambda tests use mocked awslambda, and CI definitions only specify what automation should run.
Avoid release/build cleanup scripts during source-only investigation: root build invokes remove-dist, and maintainer adapter release instructions describe committing, tagging and pushing.
